data.title: PeraMorphIQ introduced to the new intake at the E24 Induction Programme
data.Author: PeraMorphIQ Neuromorphic Research Group
data.brief: "Projects at PeraCom", organised by the Department of Computer Engineering, gave our newest undergraduates a first look at the research shaping the department, including the neuromorphic hardware work of PeraMorphIQ.
data.fullContent:
As part of the E24 student induction programme, the Department of Computer Engineering ran "Projects at PeraCom", a session giving the newest intake of undergraduates an early look at the research and projects under way across the department.
PeraMorphIQ presented alongside the other department project groups. We introduced the research group and its work on neuromorphic architectures for spiking neural networks: configurable accelerator design, RISC-V System-on-Chip and Network-on-Chip integration, and FPGA prototyping aimed at energy-efficient inference at the edge.
The session gave students the chance to talk directly with the researchers about what the group builds, how final year and graduate projects run within it, and how to get involved.
Here's to exploring possibilities, creating impact, and beginning an inspiring engineering journey.

data.title: Review paper published in the Journal of Systems Architecture
data.Author: PeraMorphIQ Neuromorphic Research Group
data.brief: Our review of neuromorphic architectures for edge-oriented spiking neural networks is published in the Journal of Systems Architecture (Elsevier, Q1), and is freely available under open access.
data.fullContent:
A review paper from the PeraMorphIQ Neuromorphic Research Group has been published in the Journal of Systems Architecture (JSA), a Q1 Elsevier journal with an impact factor of 5.3 and a CiteScore of 9.1.
"Neuromorphic architectures for edge-oriented spiking neural networks: A review" appears in Volume 177, August 2026, as article 103869. The article is open access under a Creative Commons licence.
The paper presents a comprehensive review of neuromorphic ASIC and FPGA architectures for edge-oriented spiking neural network (SNN) acceleration. It highlights the mismatch between existing hardware and the demands of small-scale, resource-constrained, real-time edge workloads; surveys neuron models, coding schemes, learning methods and on-chip communication strategies; and argues for System-on-Chip based neuromorphic platforms as a route to practical, real-time and energy-efficient edge applications.
Authors: Kanishka Gunawardana, Sanka Peeris, Kavishka Rambukwella, Prof. Roshan G. Ragel (supervisor) and Dr. Isuru Nawinne (supervisor).
Congratulations to the team, and thank you to everyone who supported this work.

data.title: Open-source release: PeraMorphIQ SRAM Compiler
data.Author: PeraMorphIQ Neuromorphic Research Group
data.brief: A streamlined, automated workflow for generating custom SRAM macros, built on the OpenRAM framework and released publicly for the open-source hardware community.
data.fullContent:
We have publicly released the PeraMorphIQ SRAM Compiler, a streamlined and automated workflow for generating custom SRAM macros, built upon the OpenRAM framework.
In developing neuromorphic accelerators and RISC-V prototypes at PeraMorphIQ we needed to create SRAM blocks easily and in a highly configurable way, integrating cleanly with modern EDA environments. This release bridges the gap between open-source research tools and industrial design requirements.
Building on the foundational work of the VLSIDA group, our implementation focuses on stability, usability and modern tool compatibility: it resolves critical circular import dependencies and compatibility issues with current Python environments; adds native support for vertical (address division) and horizontal (bit-slicing) banking through a simplified configuration; includes automated post-processing scripts that generate .db (Design Compiler) and NDM (IC Compiler II) libraries; and organises GDS, LEF, Verilog and Liberty outputs automatically for immediate interoperability with place-and-route flows.
The tool is designed to lower the barrier to entry for researchers and students designing custom silicon in the FreePDK45, Sky130 and GF180 technology nodes.
We invite the open-source hardware community to explore the repository, star the project and contribute to its development.
Acknowledgement: this work is a derivative of the OpenRAM project by VLSIDA (UCSC/OSU). We thank the original authors for their contribution to the field.

data.title: PeraMorphIQ Unveiled at the Faculty of Engineering 75th Anniversary Exhibition
data.brief: The Department of Computer Engineering at the University of Peradeniya introduced PeraMorphIQ, a new neuromorphic research initiative, during the 75th Anniversary Exhibition, marking the department’s first public showcase of brain-inspired computing research
data.Author: PeraMorphIQ Neuromorphic Research Group
data.fullContent:
As part of the 75th Anniversary Exhibition of the Faculty of Engineering, the Department of Computer Engineering proudly presented its latest advancements in computer architecture, embedded systems, and FPGA-based prototypes. The exhibition highlighted the department’s strong expertise in hardware design and real-time computing, while also unveiling an exciting new frontier for our research community: neuromorphic computing. Through the Embedded Systems and Computer Architecture Lab (ESCAL), our teams demonstrated how we are advancing beyond traditional architectures toward cognitive and brain-inspired systems that integrate intelligence, adaptability, and energy efficiency.
 The event also marked the official introduction of PeraMorphIQ, the department’s dedicated neuromorphic research group. This initiative represents a milestone in the department’s history as the first public showcase of neuromorphic computing. PeraMorphIQ aims to design energy-efficient, brain-inspired architectures, explore Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) as next-generation AI models, and pioneer on-chip learning and memory-optimized systems. The exhibition served as both a celebration of past achievements and a vision for the future, as the department continues to expand collaborations, strengthen its research ecosystem, and position ESCAL and PeraMorphIQ as hubs for cutting-edge computer architecture and neuromorphic innovation.
